description: Three-panel composite figure of finite-element (FE) simulation results for a triplex low-density steel; all three panels are line plots. (a) True stress (MPa, 0-800) versus true strain (0.00-0.21), with legend entries "Sim-damaged:" (hollow circles: "Our LDS" red, "Fe-TiB2 steel" orange), "Exp:" (filled markers with lines: Our LDS, Fe-TiB2 steel, IF steel) and "Sim-undamaged:" (solid lines: Our LDS red, Fe-TiB2 steel orange, IF steel black). The red LDS curve reaches the highest stress, ending near 750 MPa at ~0.12-0.13 strain; Fe-TiB2 ends near 600 MPa at ~0.11; IF steel near 460 MPa at ~0.18. (b) Dislocation density (10^14 m^-2, 3-21) versus true strain (0.00-0.15): simulated δ-Ferrite (red) starts near 11 and rises to ~18, simulated Austenite (blue) starts near 3 and rises to ~20; the two curves cross near strain 0.09. Experimental points (filled circles) at the highest strain: Austenite ~20 (matching simulation), δ-Ferrite ~17 (below simulation). (c) True stress in each phase (MPa, 0-1400) versus global true stress (0-1000 MPa): TiB2 (yellow) highest reaching ~1180 MPa, δ-Ferrite (red) ~710 MPa, Austenite (blue) ~670 MPa at ~830 MPa global stress, with a dashed 1:1 reference line. Together the panels show the model reproduces experiment, and that the softest phase (austenite) yields first while TiB2 carries the greatest load.

subfigures.description: True stress (MPa) versus true strain line plot, axes 0-800 MPa and 0.00-0.21. Three data families: simulation with damage (hollow circles), simulation without damage (solid lines) and experimental curves (filled markers+lines), each for 'Our LDS' (red), 'Fe-TiB2 steel' (orange) and 'IF steel' (black). The red 'Our LDS' curve is the highest, ending near 750 MPa at ~0.12-0.13 strain; orange Fe-TiB2 reaches ~600 MPa at ~0.11 strain; black IF steel ~460 MPa at ~0.18 strain.

Dislocation density (10^14 m^-2) versus true strain, axes 3-21 and 0.00-0.15. Simulated results: δ-Ferrite (red line) begins near 11 at zero strain and rises to ~18, Austenite (blue line) begins near 3 and rises to ~20; the curves cross near strain 0.09. Experimental result: δ-Ferrite (red filled circle, ~17) and Austenite (blue filled circle, ~20) at the highest strain; the austenite point matches simulation, the δ-ferrite point lies below the simulated curve. Panel label is partly cropped in the supplied image.

True stress in each phase (MPa, 0-1400) versus global true stress (MPa, 0-1000), legend 'Austenite' (blue), 'δ-Ferrite' (red), 'TiB2' (yellow), plus a dashed straight line. TiB2 shows the highest phase stress (~1180 MPa at ~830 MPa global stress), δ-ferrite intermediate (~710 MPa) and austenite the lowest (~670 MPa); the curves fan out above ~400 MPa global stress.

observations.observation: Panel (a) plots true stress (MPa) against true strain, with axes spanning 0-800 MPa and 0.00-0.21; three data families are distinguished by symbol style: 'Sim-damaged' (hollow circles), 'Exp' (filled circles with solid lines) and 'Sim-undamaged' (solid lines).

In panel (a) the red 'Our LDS' curves are the highest of the three alloys, terminating near 750 MPa at a true strain of about 0.12-0.13, above the orange 'Fe-TiB2 steel' (~600 MPa at ~0.11) and the black 'IF steel' (~460 MPa at ~0.18).

In panel (a) the simulated (hollow circles, damaged condition) data points of 'Our LDS' follow the same locus as the experimental red curve over the whole strain range, i.e. the simulation overlaps the measured tensile curve.
Panel (b) gives dislocation density in units of 10^14 m^-2 on a 3-21 scale versus true strain 0.00-0.15, starting with δ-Ferrite near 11 x10^14 m^-2 and Austenite near 3 x10^14 m^-2 at zero strain.
In panel (b) the simulated δ-Ferrite (red) and Austenite (blue) dislocation-density curves intersect near a true strain of 0.09, after which austenite accumulates dislocations faster.

In panel (b) the experimental point for Austenite at the highest strain coincides with the simulated curve (~20 x10^14 m^-2), whereas the experimental δ-Ferrite point (~17 x10^14 m^-2) falls below its simulated curve (~18 x10^14 m^-2).

Panel (c) plots true stress in each phase (MPa, 0-1400) against global true stress (MPa, 0-1000) with three curves labelled Austenite (blue), δ-Ferrite (red) and TiB2 (yellow), plus a dashed straight line; TiB2 consistently lies above the other two phases.

In panel (c) at the terminal point of the curves (global true stress just below 900 MPa) TiB2 reaches the highest phase stress (between the 1000 and 1200 MPa gridlines, close to 1200), δ-Ferrite the next (just above the 700 MPa gridline) and Austenite the lowest (just above the 600 MPa gridline).

The caption states that the present steel (labelled 'Our LDS' in the panels) is compared with 'the conventional Fe-TiB steel' and 'interstitial-free steel' under damaged (hollow circles) and undamaged (solid lines) conditions, alongside experimentally measured tensile curves.
The caption states that panel (b) shows the simulated evolution of dislocation densities in the two matrix phases of the present steel with the experimentally measured values shown for comparison.

The caption describes panel (c) as the simulated evolution of true stresses in each phase with the global true strain, whereas the printed axis of that panel reads 'Global true stress (MPa)' - the caption and axis disagree on the abscissa quantity.

The citing text states that the red curves in Fig. 11(a, b) show simulation results closely matching the experimentally measured true stress-strain curves and dislocation densities, confirming the constitutive model.

The citing text states that in Fig. 11(c) TiB2, the hardest phase, experiences the highest stress levels while austenite, the softest phase, exhibits the lowest stresses, i.e. an uneven distribution of phase stresses.

The citing text states that below a global stress of 490 MPa all phase stresses rise almost linearly (elastic stage), that the phase stress of δ-ferrite exceeds that of austenite by nearly 50% at that stage, and that yielding of the present steel starts with plastic flow of austenite rather than δ-ferrite; above 600 MPa the matrix flows plastically and above 700 MPa the δ-ferrite phase stress falls below the global true stress.

The citing text states that the austenite phase in the present steel has a low initial dislocation density and an equiaxed morphology supporting full recrystallization, whereas δ-ferrite bands show higher dislocation densities (referring to Fig. 11(c) [sic]).
